scenes.title: Where and when
narration: J-Setting emerged in 1971 at Jackson State University when Shirley Middleton and 18 majorettes requested to perform without batons.
Middleton, a ballet dancer, established the technical standards.

In 1975, Narah Oatis became the sponsor, overseeing the development of signature steps like the 'J-Sette Walk.' The style was further shaped by Hollis Pippins, an openly gay drum major who collaborated on choreography before 1975.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: J-Setting is performed during university football games, homecomings, and parades.
It has also become a vital part of Black gay pride events.
It represents a fusion of collegiate tradition and queer subculture, often described as a form of 'Black queer feminist worldmaking.'
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance uses a lead-and-follow format where a captain initiates moves for the line to follow.
Key techniques include 'bucking' (powerful body and arm thrusts) and the 'Salt and Pepper' (a high-knee prance lifting the foot to the opposite knee's height).
Dancers perform in rows based on height: 'Short & Sassy', 'Magnificent Middle', and 'Tall & Tough'.
Watch for Bucking, Salt and Pepper.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Linear rows that shift into complex geometric patterns similar to marching band drills.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The primary musical accompaniment is the Jackson State University marching band, known as the 'Sonic Boom of the South.' Early performances featured funk tracks like James Brown's 'Make it Funky' and 'Hot Pants.' The music is characterized by heavy brass and percussion typical of HBCU marching bands.
Listen for the Trumpet, Trombone, Tuba, Snare Drum.
The pulse is 4/4 at about 100 beats a minute.
The sound is dominated by the 'Sonic Boom'—a massive, brass-heavy marching band sound with a thunderous percussion section that provides a constant, driving pulse for the dancers.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performers typically wear one or two-piece bodysuits or form-fitting garments that cover the torso, paired with hosiery and knee-high boots.
While traditionally performed on football fields and in parades, the style is also prominent in gay nightclubs and competitive dance stages.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures include Shirley Middleton (founder), Hollis Pippins (choreographer and drum major), Narah Oatis (long-time sponsor), and Frank Gatson (choreographer who introduced the style to Beyoncé).
While originating in Jackson, Mississippi, the style spread across the South to cities like Mobile, Alabama, where groups like the Prancing Elites popularized their own version of the tradition.
J-Setting is a descendant of African American majorette traditions and traditional African dance movements.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: J-Setting is parent of Majorette: J-Setting evolved directly from the baton-twirling majorette tradition.
